newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's Marzotto/HPI merger wins market's approval.
newsitem.headline: Italy's Marzotto/HPI merger wins market's approval.

text.p: A plan for newly formed Italian company HPI to merge with textiles group Marzotto was welcomed on the bourse on Monday as making industrial sense, with shares in both firms trading higher.

Marzotto, which owns German clothing label Hugo Boss, and Holding Partecipazioni Industriali (HPI), which was formally spun off from financial holding Gemina last week, said late on Friday they intended to merge into new Gruppo Industriale Marzotto (GIM).
"They are two competitors who are uniting and their fire power on the world market is being more than doubled," said Antonio Tognoli of ING Bank.
HPI made its debut as a separate entity on the Milan market on Monday, with its shares trading at 1,110 lire, up 5.6 percent on the theoretical 1,050 valuation given by the bourse council.
Shares in Marzotto, which is controlled by the family of that name, were six percent higher at 14,275 lire.

Marco Nascimbeni, salesman at Merrill Lynch Capital Market Bank, said: "This is not bad news for an Italian market which suffers from having too many small companies. It will become one of the country's most important industrial holdings."

Marzotto, which has a market capitalisation about a quarter the size of HPI, will absorb the larger firm, which groups former Gemina units sportswear maker Fila and textile group GFT, which produces for designers like Giorgio Armani.
Analysts' initial assessments were upbeat, saying the main point was the deal brought together GFT and Marzotto's clothing business, creating a world class textile company.
But they said it was early days and they wanted more details from the firms.

Giordano Lombardo, analyst at Credito Italiano, said as an industrial project the plan was complementary in distribution terms, with Marzotto strong in Europe and HPI stronger in the United States with Fila. "There seems to be little duplication of business," he added.
"The businesses are already rationalised, even if there is still something to do in GFT, but that has to be done merger or no merger," Lombardo said.
Queries hung over HPI's publishing activities, which sit uneasily with the textile and apparel operations. "Investors want to know what kind of future they have," Nascimbeni said.

"The bad news is Marzotto will become a diversified industrial holding company with few synergies between components and is therefore likely to trade at a 20 percent discount to the value of its component parts," one analyst said.

The new GIM will have one trillion lire ($590 million) in net cash, which the analyst said could prompt concern that future investment would not be kept to its core activities but could be used to help its larger shareholders with their plans.
Under current stakes, the big shareholders will be Fiat with 17 percent, the Marzotto family and investment bank Mediobanca.
Nascimbeni said the advantages for HPI's Fila were not clear. "This is not something Marzotto normally produces and it's not yet clear what benefits Fila will get."
Analysts were positive about efforts to keep the operation transparent, with the instant release of the proposed share swap ratio of 13 HPI ordinary shares for one Marzotto.
"The market is favourably impressed with the ratio. It's in line with market prices, which limits the possibility of speculation and insider trading to a minimum," Nascimbeni said.
